title: What Is a Caltrop?
summary: A few centimetres of iron with four spikes, so shaped that one point always stands up. What the Romans called it, the story of buried caltrops at Gaugamela that only Curtius tells, Vegetius and the scythed chariots, Scipio's refusal, what has been dug up at Caerleon, Tyras and Enns, three myths, and what we do not know.

places.name: Gaugamela (northern Iraq)
places.note: Where Curtius says Darius buried iron spikes. The exact site of the battle is uncertain.

places.name: Caerleon (Wales)
places.note: Seventeen caltrops, fourteen of them in one room of the legionary barracks. Third century.

places.name: Newstead (Scotland)
places.note: A caltrop from the Roman fort, 1st and 2nd centuries.

places.name: Enns (Austria)
places.note: Caltrops in the Roman museum, 2nd to 4th century.

places.name: Tyras (Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, Ukraine)
places.note: Caltrops about 5 cm across from a building thought by one excavator to be an arsenal.

title: The Roman Onager: Rome's One-Armed Stone-Thrower
summary: A one-armed Roman stone-thrower, named after a wild ass, shook Persian siege towers apart at Amida in A.D. 359. How it worked, how it was crewed and carried, what it really did, and what nobody knows: the only technical description is a few sentences by one officer, and no original machine has been identified.

places.name: Maiozamalcha (near Ctesiphon, Iraq)
places.note: An engineer killed by his own machine, A.D. 363. The exact site is unknown.

title: What Was a Pugio?
summary: A coin struck by Caesar's killers shows two daggers. The pugio, Rome's short dagger, appears in the stories of Caesar, Scaevinus, Arria and Sertorius, none of them a battle. What museums hold, the 2019 dagger from Haltern with silver, enamel and glass, a real dispute about where the pugio came from, and what we do not know about how soldiers used it.

title: The Roman Scorpion: Rome's Sniper Weapon
summary: A Gaulish warrior on a burning wall is hit by a bolt from a machine he never saw. The Roman scorpion was a torsion bolt-shooter powered by twisted sinew and hair. How it worked, who built it, how deadly it was, and what the evidence can and cannot prove, from Alesia to Jotapata.
